before: JavaScript can throw values other than Error objects. Under this strict TypeScript setup, a caught value is unknown. Use a real check before reading its message.

after: `throw` stops the current work and sends a value to `catch`. That value can be an `Error` object, text, or something else. Here, its type is `unknown`, so check it before reading `.message`.
An `Error` may have an empty message. Return that empty text as it is. A plain string is not an `Error` object, even if it contains the same words. It uses the fallback message.

before.question: The caught value is the string "Door closed", not new Error("Door closed"). What does failureText return?
choices: Door closed, because all thrown values gain a message.
An empty string, because string errors disappear.
before.explanation: A thrown string stays a string. It does not satisfy instanceof Error, so the fallback branch runs.

after.question: What does `failureText` return when it catches the plain string `"Door closed"`?
choices: Door closed, because throw adds a message field.
Empty text, because the string disappears.
after.explanation: The string stays a string. It fails the `instanceof Error` check, so the fallback is returned.

project.title: Narrow a caught value before reading it
project.task: Complete `describeFailure(failure: unknown)`. Keep the practice throw and catch. Return an Error's message, including empty text. Return `"Unknown failure"` for other values.
project.done_when: Error objects keep their messages. Strings, null, and other values receive the fallback without unsafe property access.
